evidence.claim: East of Rutland, US 4 winds through the Green Mountains as a two-lane highway, passing Mendon and Killington before following the Ottauquechee River valley.
evidence.quote: East of Rutland, US 4 is a two-lane highway, meandering through the Green Mountains and passing by the towns of Mendon and Killington. In Killington, US 4 joins VT 100 as they pass through Killington along the Ottauquechee River valley until reaching West Bridgewater.

evidence.claim: Vermont Tourism includes the Crossroad of Vermont in its scenic-byway collection: a 50-mile east-west route from Rutland to the New Hampshire border, including Killington and Woodstock.
evidence.quote: Crossroad of Vermont Byway This 50-mile east-west route spans the state from Rutland to the New Hampshire border, includ ing Woodstock and Killington .

evidence.claim: The road through Rutland and Woodstock to White River Junction became Route 13 in the New England road marking system in 1922, then US 4 in late 1926.
evidence.quote: The road running from the New York state line (toward Whitehall, New York) at Fair Haven eastward through Rutland and Woodstock to White River Junction was designated as Route 13 of the New England road marking system in 1922.

evidence.claim: The road through Rutland and Woodstock to White River Junction became Route 13 in the New England road marking system in 1922, then US 4 in late 1926.

evidence.claim: The road through Rutland and Woodstock to White River Junction became Route 13 in the New England road marking system in 1922, then US 4 in late 1926.
evidence.quote: Numbered Highway System as US 4.

evidence.claim: West of Rutland, a 19-mile expressway was built for a proposed East–West Highway that never materialized.
evidence.quote: The 19-mile (31 km) US 4 expressway was built in anticipation of the proposed, but never built, East–West Highway

evidence.claim: Its final eastern segment opened in 1986, and the old surface route there became US 4 Business.
evidence.quote: The construction of the eastern segment (from exit 6 to the intersection with US 7) was delayed for several years and did not open to traffic until 1986. The original surface alignment east of exit 6 was redesignated as US 4 Bus.

evidence.claim: Eastward from Rutland, US 4 passes Mendon and Killington, then follows the Ottauquechee through Bridgewater and Woodstock.
evidence.quote: East of Rutland, US 4 is a two-lane highway, meandering through the Green Mountains and passing by the towns of Mendon and Killington.

evidence.claim: Eastward from Rutland, US 4 passes Mendon and Killington, then follows the Ottauquechee through Bridgewater and Woodstock.
evidence.quote: In Killington, US 4 joins VT 100 as they pass through Killington along the Ottauquechee River valley until reaching West Bridgewater.

evidence.claim: Eastward from Rutland, US 4 passes Mendon and Killington, then follows the Ottauquechee through Bridgewater and Woodstock.
evidence.quote: VT 100 splits off to the south while US 4 continues following the Ottauquechee River east through Bridgewater center into the town of Woodstock.

evidence.claim: Beyond Taftsville, it reaches Quechee Gorge and turns toward the White River.
evidence.quote: US 4 continues following the Ottauquechee River into Quechee, passing through the Quechee State Park and circling south of Deweys Pond to cross the river on the Quechee Gorge Bridge, before heading north to the south bank of the White River.

evidence.claim: It follows that river into White River Junction before crossing the Connecticut River into New Hampshire on the Lyman Bridge.
evidence.quote: then turns eastward following the river bank into the village of White River Junction.

evidence.claim: crossing the Connecticut River into New Hampshire on the Lyman Bridge
evidence.quote: US 4 crosses the New Hampshire state line at the Connecticut River on the Lyman Bridge

evidence.claim: Pico Peak stands south of Sherburne Pass, with Deer Leap Mountain to the north.
evidence.quote: between 3,957-foot (1,206 m) Pico Peak to the south and 2,782-foot (848 m) Deer Leap Mountain to the north.

evidence.claim: The pass divides two drainage systems: eastward water reaches the Ottauquechee and Connecticut rivers, then Long Island Sound.
evidence.quote: On the east side, the pass drains into Kent Brook, thence into the Ottauquechee River, the Connecticut River, and into Long Island Sound in Connecticut.

evidence.claim: Westward water reaches Lake Champlain and eventually the Saint Lawrence.
evidence.quote: thence into Lake Champlain. Lake Champlain drains into the Richelieu River in Québec, thence into the Saint Lawrence River

evidence.claim: The Appalachian and Long trails once crossed Route 4 at the height of the pass.
evidence.quote: The AT and LT formerly crossed Rt. 4 at the height of Sherburne Pass

evidence.claim: Both moved to Pico’s west slope; their former route is now the blue-blazed Sherburne Pass Trail.
evidence.quote: Both were moved to the west slope of the mountain. The old route of the AT/LT is now a blue-blazed trail, named the Sherburne Pass Trail.

evidence.claim: From the pass, Pico Peak’s summit has the shape of a cone.
evidence.quote: Seen from the pass, the summit of Pico Peak resembles a cone.

evidence.claim: Three bridges at this Ottauquechee crossing fell to floods, in 1807, 1811 and 1828.
evidence.quote: The first bridge was washed away during a flood in 1807, with its replacement also falling to floodwaters in 1811. When the third bridge at the site was again washed away during an 1828 flood

evidence.claim: Solomon Emmons III was then contracted to build a more resilient crossing, completing the timber-framed covered bridge in 1836.
evidence.quote: Solomon Emmons III was contracted to build a more resilient crossing. His timber-framed, covered bridge was completed in 1836

evidence.claim: That bridge survives.
evidence.quote: still stands today as the modern Taftsville Bridge.

evidence.claim: Hurricane Irene badly damaged it in 2011, and it reopened in September 2013 after two years of repairs.
evidence.quote: The Taftsville Bridge was extensively damaged by flooding caused by Hurricane Irene in 2011, and was closed for two years while repairs took place. It was reopened in September 2013.

evidence.claim: Its two spans meet at a central pier in the river gorge.
evidence.quote: with two spans of 89 feet (27 m) and 100 feet (30 m) from either river bank to a central pier in the river gorge.

evidence.claim: Quechee Gorge is Vermont’s deepest gorge, a 165-foot cut along US 4.
evidence.quote: The Quechee Gorge is located in Quechee, Vermont along U.S. Route 4. The gorge is 165 feet deep and is the deepest gorge in Vermont.

evidence.claim: The Ottauquechee runs along its bottom.
evidence.quote: The Ottauquechee River flows through the bottom of the gorge

evidence.claim: The gorge formed approximately 13,000 years ago as the Laurentide Ice Sheet withdrew.
evidence.quote: The gorge was carved approximately 13,000 years ago as the Laurentide Ice Sheet retreated across the region.

evidence.claim: Its carving is thought to have followed the draining of glacial Lake Hitchcock, when the Ottauquechee rapidly cut downward.
evidence.quote: The carving is thought to be a result of rapid downcutting of the Ottauquechee River after the drainage of glacial Lake Hitchcock.

evidence.claim: The cut exposes bedrock of the Devonian Gile Mountain Formation, with Mesozoic mafic dikes visible on the west wall.
evidence.quote: The gorge cuts through bedrock of the Devonian Gile Mountain Formation and Mesozoic mafic dikes can be seen on the west wall.

evidence.claim: The gorge is visible from the US 4 bridge and trails on both sides.
evidence.quote: can be viewed from the U.S. Route 4 bridge and from trails on both sides of the gorge.

evidence.claim: At Sherburne Pass, the crossing lies between Pico Peak and Deer Leap Mountain; farther east, Quechee Gorge drops 165 feet beneath the surrounding land.
evidence.quote: Sherburne Pass, is a mountain pass in the Green Mountains of Vermont, between 3,957-foot (1,206 m) Pico Peak to the south and 2,782-foot (848 m) Deer Leap Mountain to the north.

evidence.claim: Quechee Gorge drops 165 feet
evidence.quote: The gorge is 165 feet deep

evidence.claim: At Quechee, the highway bridge itself offers a view into the gorge.
evidence.quote: can be viewed from the U.S. Route 4 bridge

evidence.claim: The western ascent begins in Mendon, while the height of land lies within Killington, with the east side draining through Kent Brook and the west through Mendon Brook.
evidence.quote: The height of land of the pass is located in the town of Killington, while its western ascent begins in the town of Mendon.

evidence.claim: The village’s mills had created the need for a river crossing. Stephen Taft and his brother established them within a decade of his arrival in the early 1790s.
evidence.quote: Stephen Taft, after whom the village was ultimately named, arrived in the early 1790s. Within a decade of Taft's arrival, he and his brother had established a number of mills and the increasingly busy settlement required a bridge over the Ottauquechee River.

evidence.claim: with the east side draining through Kent Brook and the west through Mendon Brook.
evidence.quote: On the east side, the pass drains into Kent Brook

evidence.claim: the west through Mendon Brook
evidence.quote: To the west, the pass drains via Mendon Brook
